native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 cohort data, individuals jailed between 1985 and 1994 (ever_jailed=1) had significantly lower composite wealth than never-jailed individuals in all three measured years (1985, 1990, 1996; all p < 1.6e-10 across Welch t, log1p-transformed Welch t, and Mann-Whitney U tests, robust to removing 1,899 duplicate rows). The largest and most question-relevant gaps occur post-incarceration in 1990 and 1996, where the jailed group's median wealth was $0 versus $10,500 and $8,500 for the never-jailed (mean gaps of $57,598 and $85,063, i.e., jailed-group means only ~22% and ~19% of the comparison group). The 1985 gap (median $720 vs $3,600) was measured before/within the incarceration window and is therefore better interpreted as pre-existing socioeconomic disadvantage (selection) rather than a consequence of incarceration. Hypothesis (correlational, not causal): having a criminal record is associated with substantially and significantly lower wealth in the post-incarceration years 1990 and 1996 — and this pattern holds across race and sex subgroups — while the 1985 deficit reflects prior disadvantage. The dataset cannot support a causal claim because confounders such as education and earnings history are unavailable.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows x 6 cols, zero missingness). 2) Main analysis: compared ever_jailed=1 (n=289) vs ever_jailed=0 (n=11,724) on composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996 using (a) Welch t-test on raw values, (b) Welch t-test on log1p-transformed values, (c) two-sided Mann-Whitney U; reported group means, medians, SDs, mean and median differences. 3) Duplicate-row sensitivity: dropped 1,899 exact duplicates (n=10,114; jailed n=239) and reran all tests; conclusions identical across all years and tests. 4) Stratified analyses by race (white n1=69, black n1=159, hipanic n1=61) and sex (male n1=252, female n1=37), with small subgroups treated descriptively. 5) Aggregated per-year significance and formulated the natural-language hypothesis with interpretation boundary for the 1985 baseline (pre/within incarceration window). Outputs: outputs/main_results.csv, outputs/dedup_sensitivity_results.csv, outputs/analysis_output.txt.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.

sub_hypo.text: In the NLSY79 cohort, individuals jailed between 1985 and 1994 had significantly lower composite wealth in 1985 than individuals not jailed during that window. Median wealth was $720 versus $3,600. Because 1985 precedes or falls within the incarceration window, this deficit is interpreted as pre-existing socioeconomic disadvantage rather than a consequence of incarceration.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 cohort; wealth measured in 1985, before or within the 1985–1994 incarceration window. Results were robust to removing 1,899 duplicate rows.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed individuals had lower 1985 wealth: median $720 versus $3,600; p < 1.6e-10 across raw-value Welch t, log1p-transformed Welch t, and two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests. The association reflects prior disadvantage rather than an established incarceration effect.

sub_hypo.text: In the NLSY79 cohort, having been jailed between 1985 and 1994 was associated with substantially and significantly lower composite wealth in 1990 and 1996, the years characterized as post-incarceration in the hypothesis. These are correlational, not causal, associations.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 cohort; comparisons of individuals jailed versus not jailed during 1985–1994, using wealth measured in 1990 and 1996. Results were robust to removing 1,899 duplicate rows. Education and earnings history were unavailable, preventing causal claims.
sub_hypo.relations: The largest wealth gaps occurred in 1990 and 1996: jailed-group median wealth was $0 in both years versus $10,500 and $8,500, respectively. Mean wealth was lower by $57,598 and $85,063, with jailed-group means approximately 22% and 19% of comparison-group means. All p < 1.6e-10 across raw-value Welch t, log1p-transformed Welch t, and two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests; association does not establish causation.

sub_hypo.text: The association between having been jailed between 1985 and 1994 and lower wealth in 1990 and 1996 held across race and sex subgroups in the NLSY79 cohort.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 cohort stratified separately by race (white, black, Hispanic) and sex (male, female); small subgroups were treated descriptively.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed individuals had lower wealth in 1990 and 1996 across race and sex subgroups. This is a correlational pattern; subgroup-specific statistical significance is not asserted.
